notes.text: You can answer d4 with d5, but in the King's Indian you develop a knight first.
notes.original: The King's Indian Defense starts with d4. Black can choose to meet up in the center with d5 but instead, black develops their knight.

notes.text: Your knight develops, and you plan to fianchetto the bishop and get your king out of the center quickly.
notes.original: Black develops their knight and plans to fianchetto their bishop and get their king out of the center as soon as possible.

notes.text: White takes more of the center with c4; you carry on with your plan to fianchetto the bishop.
notes.original: White will usually take advantage of this will take further control of the center with the move, c4. Black should continue with their plan to fianchetto their bishop.

notes.text: Bf4 instead of c4 is the London System; you can play d5 or g6 for a King's Indian.
notes.original: Instead of c4, white plays Bf4 which leads to the London System. Here black can respond classically with d5 and enter the main lines or they can play g6 and enter the King's Indian Defense.

notes.text: The Trompowsky bishop hits your knight at once; you usually avoid doubled pawns.
notes.original:
The Trompowsky Attack is a new offbeat opening with less theory which involves White immediately putting the bishop on g5 attacking the knight. Usually in most variations (2...Ne4 or 2...e6) Black avoids doubled pawns, but sometimes accepts them (2...c5 or 2...d5). The latter of each pair (2...e6 or 2...d5) just mentioned can transpose into the Torre Attack after 3.Nf3; however the Trompowsky Main Line (2...Ne4) typically doesn't transpose after it's played.In the Trompowsky Main Line, both sides move their developed minor piece twice: Black's knight from g8 to f6 to e4 and White's Bishop from c1 to g5 to f4. Afterward Black has many options to develop unlike many other openings. Some possible developing moves include c5, d5, d6, or e6.

A less common but also popular line involves 2...e6 (Classical Defense) when it is best not to trade pieces and instead develop naturally. This line can transpose into the Torre Attack with 3.Nf3 or continue with 3.e4 in the Trompowsky (Big Center Variation, which fits the position perfectly) and Black usually avoids the trade of minor pieces because of the pin (h6 and e5) and instead trades pieces directly with 4.Bxf6.

Even less common but transposable is the move 2...d5 which asks for a transposition into the Torre Attack (3.Nf3) or the Richter-Veresov (3.Nc3) but White can take advantage of the move and stay in the Trompowsky with 3.Bxf6, doubling Black's pawns.

Less common again is the 2...c5 line attacking the pawn. White can choose to push the pawn or trade pieces (3.d5 or 3.Bxf6). The former variation involves a "Poisoned Pawn Variation" which involves one side giving away a pawn for a opposing misplaced queen and a development lead. The variation goes 2...c5 3.d5 Qb6 4.Nc3 Qxb2.

There is also the move 2...c6!?, which is less commonly played, but nonetheless quite sound. This could lead to similar positions as the 2...c5 line, related to the poisoned pawn variation, or this can lead to 1.d4 openings, such as the Richter-Veresov Attack or even the QGD/Slav Defenses. This line also contains a trap: white must be careful and avoid 3.e3??, where 3...Qa5+ loses the bishop on g5 to a fork.

notes.text: The g6 pawn opens g7 for your bishop, which will aim down the long diagonal.
notes.original: Black opens up the g7 square for their bishop and plans to put it on the long diagonal.

notes.text: White wants e4 to take the whole center, but needed to develop this knight first.
notes.original: White wants to play e4 and take full control of the center, but has to develop the knight first before doing so.

notes.text: With the knight on f3, White gives up the aggressive Four Pawns Attack and the Sämisch.
notes.original: White develops a piece and continues their fight for the central dark squares. This Knight's development, while solid, prevents White's option of playing f3 or f4 and thus gives up options of the aggressive Four Pawns Attack by requiring f4 and the Samisch, which requires f3.

notes.text: This is the King's Indian setup: you give up the center for quick development and plan to castle soon.
notes.original: We have now reached the starting position of the King's Indian. Black has surrendered control of the center but has achieved quick development. Black is playing for a win here and also intends to get their king out of the center as soon as possible.

notes.text: White takes control of the center with e4.
notes.original: White should take control of the center.

notes.text: This keeps both the King's Indian and Grünfeld open; for the Grünfeld, play d5 right away.
notes.original: This Knight development is solid but leaves the options open for Black to either play The King's Indian or the Grunfeld Defence. If Black wishes to play the Grunfeld then responding immediately with d5 is required as white next move is likely to be 5.e4 which prevents d5 from being played.

notes.text: Play d6 just before castling; this is the normal King's Indian setup.
notes.original: Just before black castles, black should play d6. I will cover the variations of the King's Indian in separate chapters. Right now, this is considered to be the normal variation of the King's Indian Defense.

notes.text: In the Four Pawns Attack, White adds a fourth center pawn with f4.
notes.original: In the 4 pawns attack, white plays f4!

notes.text: This leads to the Classical, or Orthodox, King's Indian; White is simply developing and preparing to get the king out.
notes.original: This is move is known to lead up to the start of the Classical a.k.a. the Orthodox Variation of the King's Indian. White is simply developing and is preparing to get their king out of the center.

notes.text: In the Sämisch, White supports the center with the f-pawn instead of the knight.
notes.original: Now I will be showing you the Sämisch Variation of the King's Indian Defense. In this variation, white reinforces their center with the f-pawn rather than the knight going to f3.

notes.text: Castle your king.
notes.original: King

notes.text: White goes for an aggressive setup with four pawns in the centre, the Four Pawns Attack.
notes.original: here white goes for a aggressive setup. this is called the four pawns attack

notes.text: You let White develop and castle quickly yourself.
notes.original: Black simply allows white to develop and castles quickly.

notes.text: This starts the Orthodox Defense; White is preparing to castle.
notes.original: This is now the start of the Orthodox Defense. White is preparing to get their king out of the center.

notes.text: Be3 instead of Be2 is known as the Larsen Variation.
notes.original: Now we will see what happens when White doesn't make Be2 as the sixth move, and makes Be3. This play is known as the Larsen variant.

notes.text: Your e5 pawn challenges the center; White has several options, but simply castling is best.
notes.original: Now black will start to challenge the center with the move e5. White has multiple options here but his best move is to just castle.

notes.text: White castles, which is the best move here.
notes.original: White should do so.

notes.text: Now see what happens when White closes the centre with d5.
notes.original: Now we will see what happens when White decides to close the center with d5.

notes.text: Your knight develops and eyes d4, but White will want to challenge it with d5.
notes.original: Black simply develops one of their pieces and wants to start a king-side attack. White should not let this knight go unchallenged.

notes.text: White's pawn challenges your knight, which has to move.
notes.original: White simply challenges the knight, the knight is forced to move.

notes.text: The knight retreats to its most active square, supporting f5, your main idea.
notes.original: Black simply has to move their knight but this is also the most active square for their knight. This knight supports the move, f5 which is black's main idea.

notes.text: The Bayonet Attack is very aggressive: you attack on the kingside, White on the queenside, mostly in forcing lines.
notes.original: This is the beginning of the Bayonet Attack. White doesn't have to play this move, but we will be covering this move in this chapter. This is an extremely aggressive move for white and it requires extreme precision from both sides. This also gives a tremendous amount of attacking chances. Black is going to try to attack on the king-side, meanwhile white is going to try to attack on the queen-side. The good thing about the Bayonet Attack is that most lines are extremely forcing, so you probably will not see much variation in your games.

notes.text: This is the main line: you prepare f5 to start a kingside counter-attack.
notes.original: This is considered to be the main line. Black wants to prepare to play f5 and start a counter-attack on the king-side.

notes.text: The a-pawn push is the second most common move, odd as it strikes where White has most space.
notes.original: This is an alternative to Nh5. It's counter-intuitive because it's striking where white has the most space. However, this is black's 2nd most common move.

notes.text: This is the most aggressive way to meet the Bayonet Attack, and Nakamura has used it with great success.
notes.original: This is the most aggressive way to play against the Bayonet Attack. Hikaru Nakamura uses this variation to great success against the Bayonet Attack. You can see his games against Viswanathan Anand and Veselin Topalov.

notes.text: White centralizes the rook.
notes.original: White now centralizes the rook.

notes.text: Your f5 starts the kingside attack, and White does not want to take it.
notes.original: Now black starts their king-side attack with f5. Note that white does NOT want to take here.

notes.text: White's knight jumps to g5 to use the weak e6 square your f5 pawn created.
notes.original: White should instead play Ng5. The point of this move is that white wants to exploit the weakness that black created for themselves on e6.

notes.text: Taking the pawn on f5 loses immediately for White if you find the only good reply.
notes.original: If white takes the pawn, they are immediately losing if black plays the only good move in the position..

notes.text: Retreat your knight to f6 so White's bishop can't win it and ruin your kingside attack.
notes.original: Black's next move has to be Nf6. This is because black doesn't want to allow white's bishop to capture the knight and for the king-side attack to be ruined. Here white has two moves that are usually played.

notes.text: Bf3 is the most common move; now you undermine White's center and slow its kingside attack.
notes.original: Bf3 is the most common move. This now give black a different strategy in which now, black will try to undermine white's center and halts the king-side attack.

notes.text: f3 is a sideline that leads to a very sharp line both sides must know.
notes.original: f3 is a sideline in the position and this leads to a very sharp line that both sides must know.

notes.text: Play c6 to undermine White's center by hitting the d5 pawn.
notes.original: Black should do this with c6.

notes.text: White simply continues developing with the bishop to e3.
notes.original: White should continue their development with Be3.

notes.text: Play h6 to chase away White's knight on g5.
notes.original: Now black should play h6, chasing away the knight.

notes.text: White's knight lands on e6 as planned, and you should take it.
notes.original: The knight should go to e6 as planned.

notes.text: Capture the knight on e6 with your bishop.
notes.original: The only move for black is to capture this knight.

notes.text: White recaptures, but the pawn on e6 is now loose.
notes.original: White should obviously recapture. White now has a very loose pawn on e6.

notes.text: Continue by taking the e4 pawn with your f-pawn.
notes.original: Black then continues with fxe4.

notes.text: White should take with the knight; taking with the bishop would give you an edge.
notes.original: The knight should capture here, capturing with the bishop would give black an edge.

notes.text: Capture White's knight on e4 with your knight.
notes.original: Black should now capture the knight in this position.

notes.text: White recaptures the knight with the bishop.
notes.original: White should obviously recapture the knight.

notes.text: Strike with d5 to open the position, take a stand in the center and gain space.
notes.original: Black can now continue with d5. Black needs to play this move because now they have an opportunity to open up the position and take a stand in the center, creating more space for black.

notes.text: White's best is to capture the d5 pawn.
notes.original: Capturing this pawn is best for white.

notes.text: Recapture on d5; White then usually plays one of two moves.
notes.original: Black should recapture. From here two moves are usually played.

notes.text: White's bishop retreats to c2, getting out of danger.
notes.original: Bc2 is most common, getting the bishop out of danger.

notes.text: b6 looks strange, but it covers c5 against a White bishop sacrifice aimed at your d-pawn.
notes.original: b6 is the best move here. This move may look strange but the threat is Bc5 in which white can give up the bishop to potentially win the d-pawn.

notes.text: White's queen and bishop both hit your g6 pawn, while the queen also protects the e6 pawn.
notes.original: Here white plays Qg4, double attacking black's g-pawn and simultaneously defending the loose e-pawn.

notes.text: Push e4 to cut White's bishop off from your g6 pawn.
notes.original: e4 is the best move for black, cutting off the bishop to the pawn.

notes.text: White's rook pins your d5 pawn to the queen, so Bxe4 is coming.
notes.original: White can now put pressure on the d-pawn and threaten to play Bxe4. This is because the pawn will be pinned to the queen.

notes.text: Your queen connects the rooks and attacks the bishop on c2.
notes.original: Qc7 is the only move for black. This move connects the rooks and also threatens to capture the bishop.

notes.text: White's bishop and rook now both attack your d5 pawn.
notes.original: Now Bb3 is played, double attacking the d-pawn.

notes.text: Your rook protects d5. You stand slightly better, but watch your king safety.
notes.original: Rf5 is most commonly played, protecting the d-pawn. From here the game branches out as there are many moves that white can play. I have highlighted possible ideas for black in green. In my opinion, black stands better here and the only thing that black needs to be weary of is king safety.

notes.text: White's rook is heading to d2 or c2.
notes.original: I will continue with the main line but like I said, the game can branch out I think the position is not too complicated to play from this point. But if you're like me and you like to outplay your opponent with theory then here you go. The point of this move is to either play Rd2 or Rc2.

notes.text: Your h-pawn attacks White's queen.
notes.original: Black should attack the queen in this position.

notes.text: White's queen most likely retreats to h4.
notes.original: The queen will most likely move to h4.

notes.text: If White's queen drops to g3, the game should be a draw by repetition.
notes.original: If the queen drops to g3, then this game should be a draw by repetition as well.

notes.text: If White's queen drops to h3, you have a very slight edge.
notes.original: If the queen drops to h3 however.. then black now has a very slight edge.

notes.text: You can repeat moves here; the position is completely equal.
notes.original: Here black can try to get a repetition of moves as the position is completely equal. All games have ended in a draw in this position either by mutual agreement or by repetition. Feel free to evaluate how to play if white choose not to repeat however.

notes.text: Your bishop attacks White's queen, so it has to step away again.
Trading queens is fine for you; White is more likely to go wrong in the endgame.
notes.original: If black really wants to, they can go for the queen trade here which is perfectly fine, as I think there's more of a chance of white going wrong than black when the queens are off the board. We have entered the territory in which this is no longer theory and I will just show best moves for each side.

notes.text: The game ends in a draw by repetition.
White's best recapture is with the h-pawn.
notes.original: White's best move is to recapture with the h-pawn.

notes.text: Whatever White recaptures with, your rook takes control of the open c-file.
notes.original: Regardless of how white recaptures, black should play Rc8, taking control of the open file.

notes.text: White doubles rooks to target your d5 pawn.
notes.original: White should continue with Red2, targeting the d-pawn.

notes.text: Your bishop heads for a trade, simplifying the position further.
notes.original: The best move for black is to play Bg5, preparing to simplify the position even further.

notes.text: White takes your bishop; you will recapture.
notes.original: White can take this bishop.

notes.text: You recapture the bishop with your rook.
notes.original: Black should recapture.

notes.text: White takes the d5 pawn, starting a mass simplification.
notes.original: Now a mass simplification will occur when white captures the pawn with the bishop.

notes.text: Recapture the bishop with your knight.
notes.original: Black should recapture with the knight.

notes.text: White recaptures the knight with the rook.
notes.original: White will obviously recapture the knight.

notes.text: Taking the rook is your only move.
notes.original: The ONLY move for black is to take the rook now.

notes.text: The position is simplified, and with correct play from you it should almost surely be a draw.
notes.original: Now the position has been simplified, the position is almost guaranteed to be a draw if black plays correctly.

notes.text: Your king must go to f8 so White's pawn can never promote.
notes.original: Kf8 must be played by black, preventing the pawn from ever promoting.

notes.text: White's rook prepares to push the pawn and also threatens to take your a-pawn.
notes.original: Rd7 may be played, preparing to push the pawn and is also threatening to take the a-pawn.

notes.text: Your best move is a5, so the rook can no longer capture your a-pawn.
notes.original: Black's best move is a5, preventing it from being captured by the rook.

notes.text: White takes the pawn, but your b-pawn can take it back.
notes.original: White should take the pawn.

notes.text: You should recapture on a5 to win the pawn back.
notes.original: Black should recapture.

notes.text: White will most likely push the pawn to e7 with check.
notes.original: e7+ will most likely be played now.

notes.text: Ke8 is best: your king stops the pawn in its tracks.
notes.original: The best move is Ke8, stopping the pawn in its tracks.

notes.text: White's rook now eyes your a-pawn, and after Kxe7 Re5 with check would follow.
notes.original: White can play Rd5, attacking both the e-pawn after Kxe7 and Re5+ and the a-pawn.

notes.text: Throw in this check to keep White's king from ever reaching the center.
notes.original: I suggest that black throws in this check, keeping the king from ever coming to the center.

notes.text: Kh2 is White's only move against the check.
notes.original: Only move for white.

notes.text: Now you should capture the e-pawn with your king.
notes.original: Now black should capture the e-pawn.

notes.text: White checks your king and hits the e4 pawn at once, removing your most valuable asset.
notes.original: White should now check the king, forking the pawn e-pawn and the king. White wants to get rid of black's most valuable asset right now.

notes.text: Play Kf7 to keep your king close to your pawns.
notes.original: Kf7 should be played, staying close to the pawns.

notes.text: White now captures your e-pawn.
notes.original: Now white will capture the e-pawn.

notes.text: Your rook hits both the a2 and f2 pawns; the game should be an easy draw.
notes.original: Black should play Rc2, attacking both pawns. I will stop here because the game should be a very easy draw that I believe in intermediate players can convert. Feel free to evaluate further.

notes.text: Your bishop attacks White's queen and chases it off g3.
Your rooks double on the f-file, White's attack is neutralized, and you only need to watch your backward d-pawn.
notes.original: Black can now double up the rooks along the f-file. Black is perfectly fine in this position. White's attack is neutralized for now and the only thing black needs to be weary of now is the backward d-pawn. I have highlighted black's ideas.

notes.text: This odd king move frees g8, and a rook usually goes there to join the attack.
notes.original: Here black plays a really strange move but a very useful move. This opens up the g8 square for any of black's pieces to go to. Black usually will play Rg8 in the future to help in the attack.

notes.text: White's rook joins the attack and backs up the queenside pawn march.
notes.original: White gets their rook in the attack and prepares to continue the queen-side march.

notes.text: Your pawn kicks the knight off g5.
notes.original: This moves kicks out the knight.

notes.text: White's knight lands on e6, the square it wanted.
notes.original: Now white plants the knight on e6 like they wanted.

notes.text: You capture the knight on e6 with your bishop, and White must recapture.
notes.original: The only move for white is to capture the knight with the bishop.

notes.text: White recaptures, but the pawn on e6 is loose and may fall later.
notes.original: Now white has to recapture the d-pawn. Notice that d-pawn is very loose and can be recaptured at some point.

notes.text: You continue by capturing the pawn on e4.
notes.original: Now black should continue the game by capturing the e-pawn.

notes.text: White recaptures with the f-pawn, leaving doubled, isolated pawns on the e-file.
notes.original: White should recapture with the f-pawn. Now white has two isolated pawns on d-pawns.

notes.text: Develop your knight and aim it at d4, where White's weak pawns can't challenge it.
notes.original: Now black needs to play Nc6 now that the d6 pawn is gone. Note that black doesn't want to capture the knight when it goes to d5 or else the pawns will be reconnected. As for white's weakness, black wants to plant their knight on the d4 square.

notes.text: White's knight lands on d5, and you shouldn't take it with your knight.
notes.original: Now white plants their knight on d5, knowing that it really shouldn't be captured by the black knight.

notes.text: Your knight retreats to g8, a square the king move freed; it may later go to e7 or f6.
notes.original: Instead black should play Ng8 which was usefully provided by Kh8. Sometimes the knight will reroute to e7 and it sometimes goes back to f6 depending on what white does.

notes.text: White's bishop protects the loose pawns on e4 and c4.
notes.original: White should play Bd3, protecting both loose pawns.

notes.text: Your knight reaches d4, the outpost you wanted.
notes.original: Now black successfully achieves planting their knight on d4.

notes.text: White's queen eyes your loose g6 pawn while guarding the e6 pawn.
notes.original: The only move for white that doesn't give black a slight edge in Qg4, looking at the loose g-pawn and protecting the e6 pawn.

notes.text: Pushing the pawn to g5 is your best way to save it; White has two main replies.
notes.original: g5 is black's best move to defend this pawn. Here there are two main moves for white.

notes.text: White piles more pressure on your g5 pawn.
notes.original: Now white applies further pressure to this pawn with h4.

notes.text: Your knight returns to f6 and attacks the queen.
notes.original: Now the knight will come back to f6, attacking the queen.

notes.text: White's queen drops back to g3, out of danger.
notes.original: The queen should drop back to g3, getting out of danger.

notes.text: You finally win the e6 pawn, and this knight also guards g5.
notes.original: Now the e-pawn can finally be captured. This knight also defends the g5 square.

notes.text: White captures on g5, and you have two good replies.
notes.original: White should continue with hxg5. Here there are two moves for black.

notes.text: Pushing the knight to h5 is the most common choice here, and the engine slightly prefers it.
notes.original: Nh5 is the most common move and the engine likes it slightly more.

notes.text: Taking the knight on d5 is another option for you, and White then has three possible replies.
notes.original: Black can also just take the knight on d5 now that there is now passed e-pawn. White can play three moves here.

notes.text: Recapturing with the c-pawn is the most common move here.
notes.original: cxd5 is the most common move here.

notes.text: Taking the h-pawn is arguably better for White, since a central pawn will soon recapture the knight.
notes.original: Arguably a better move for white is to capture the h-pawn. This is because white's chances will probably be diminished after one of the central pawns recapture the knight.

notes.text: Your bishop escapes danger, but it must keep guarding g7, where White's queen would mate. Your g-file is now useful.
notes.original: Bf6 is the best move for black, getting the bishop out of danger. Another thing you have to keep in mind with the black pieces now is that the g7 square is mate if black ever moves the bishop. Once again, we can see how useful the move, Kh8 was. Black can use the g-file now to their own advantage.

notes.text: White's only move is to recapture on d5 with the e-pawn.
notes.original: The only move for white is to capture with the e-pawn.

notes.text: Your bishop hits White's queen, and the rook on e1 stands behind it.
notes.original: Black can create a counter threat in this position with Bh4, attacking the queen and the rook.

notes.text: The queen steps to g4, White's only move, but your bishop can still take the rook.
notes.original: Qg4 is the only move for white.

notes.text: Now your bishop should take the rook on e1.
notes.original: Now the bishop should capture the rook.

notes.text: White's only move is to recapture on e6 with the pawn, creating another passed pawn.
notes.original: Again, the only move for white is to capture with the e-pawn, getting another passed pawn.

notes.text: White cannot take with the queen, because your Qh4 creates several mate threats.
notes.original: White cannot capture with the queen in this position because of Qh4. This creates multiple mate threats. I'll show the line briefly.

notes.text: Checking the king with your bishop is your only move.
notes.original: Only move for black is to check the king.

notes.text: Kf1 is White's best, since on the h-file you could force a queen exchange. White has no real discoveries.
notes.original: The best move for white is to play Kf1. This is because if the king goes on the h-file, black can force a queen exchange. This looks scary but white doesn't really have any useful discoveries.

notes.text: Your bishop gets to safety, and your rook now checks White's king.
notes.original: Now black should play Bh4+, getting the bishop to safety and checking the king.

notes.text: The king returns to g1, and you can repeat moves here, which is the suggestion.
notes.original: The king should go back to g1. Here black can repeat moves which I suggest. I will stop the line here. Feel free to evaluate further.

notes.text: Your pawn attacks the knight on c3, which is pinned, and your king's bishop wins material.
notes.original: e4 immediately wins for black because black is attacking the knight on c3 which is pinned to the rook and the knight on f3. You can really see the power of the King's Indian bishop in this position.

notes.text: White prepares for you to take the b4 pawn by putting the bishop on a3.
notes.original: White prepares for black to take the pawn with Ba3.

notes.text: Simply take the pawn on b4.
notes.original: Black should just take the pawn.

notes.text: White had to recapture. Your rook gets the open a-file, but your real play is on the kingside.
notes.original: White has to recapture or they're losing a piece. Now black has an open file for their rook, but black will continue to attack on the king-side momentarily.

notes.text: This knight move prepares your kingside attack and the f5 pawn push.
notes.original: Black prepares for their king-side attack and prepares to play the move, f5.

notes.text: White pushes the a-pawn and keeps pressing on the queenside.
notes.original: White is also continuing with their main plan which is to start an attack on the king-side.

notes.text: Before playing f5, you put your bishop on a more active diagonal.
notes.original: Just before black plays f5, black gets their bishop on more active diagonal.

notes.text: White keeps marching its pawns on the queenside.
notes.original: White continues their pawn march on the queen-side.

notes.text: At last your kingside attack starts, and the f5 pawn hits e4.
notes.original: Black finally starts their king-side attack on white.

notes.text: White sees fxe4 coming and prepares for it by guarding e4 with the bishop.
notes.original: White realizes that fxe4 is a possibility so they prepare for this with Bd3.

notes.text: This quiet king move is prophylactic and flexible; later your knight or rook may want g8.
notes.original: This is considered to be a prophylactic and a multi-purpose move. In some lines, black will want their knight on g8 or they might even want their rook on g8.

notes.text: White activates and centralizes its rook.
notes.original: White continues with activating and centralizing their rook.

notes.text: Your knight is more active now, eyeing e4 and g4; all your pieces aim at the kingside.
notes.original: Black is getting their knight on a much more active square and black's knight is also looking at the e4 and g4 square in the future. As you can see, all of black's pieces are positioned for king-side attack.

notes.text: Both sides attack on opposite wings and mostly ignore each other; that is the Bayonet Attack's purpose.
notes.original: Now we can really see the purpose of the Bayonet Attack. Both players are attacking at opposite sides and yet, neither side does much to try to stop their opponent and each side primarily focuses on their own attack.

notes.text: The tension has cooled, and both sides have clear strengths and weaknesses.
notes.original: At this point, the tension has cooled down but we can see that their are numerous strengths and weaknesses on both sides.

notes.text: The knight guards e4 and lets White support that square with f3 or Bf3.
notes.original: This is a very important move because it not only defends the e4 pawn but more importantly, it allows white to play either f3 or Bf3 to defend the e4 square.

notes.text: This looks pointless, but it frees f8 for your bishop to defend against White's kingside attack.
notes.original: This move seems very pointless but it's an extremely important move because it allow s the bishop to go to f8 which is to help defend against white's king-side attack.

notes.text: White's pawns are getting dangerous; in the Bayonet, the side that pushes pawns harder usually gains the edge.
notes.original: As you can see, white's pawn chain is getting very dangerous. This is a common theme in the Bayonet Attack. Basically, whichever side pushes their pawns more aggressively will most likely gain an advantage.

notes.text: Against the London bishop, you answer with g6 and head for a King's Indian setup.
notes.original: I will only be going over 2..g6 in this study.

notes.text: Your main tries are c5 or e6; c5 and Qb6 hit b2, which White's early bishop left loose.
notes.original:
After 2...d5, the most common reply, the two move orders (1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Nf6 and 1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 d5) merge. Then, Black's main approaches are 3...c5 or 3...e6.

Black's most common approach to combating the Accelerated London is with both Nf6 and d5, whether they began with the Indian defence 1...Nf6 or the Closed game 1...d5.

White's plans in the London system are generally to to play e3, c3, Nd2, Bd3 in some order, and plant their kingside knight on e5 via Nf3.

3.e3 is the most common move order. This defends d4 and prepares to develop Bd3.Once Nf3 is played, e.g. 3.Nf3, the opening has converged with the regular, non-accelerated London. 3.Nc3, instead of playing c3, transposes to the Rapport-Jobava London.

Black's two main approaches involve 3...c5 or 3...e6.

The idea behind the 3...e6 line is to play 4...Bd6, getting ready to castle quickly and threatening to trade off White's London bishop. White can drop their bishop back to g2, inviting Black to trade but after hxg2 White gets the semi-open h-file in return. In the e6 lines, Black's light square bishop often has difficulty developing. This approach resembles a Semi-Slav defence with colours reversed.

The ...c5 line has the idea to to prioritise ...Bf5 and ...Qb6 before finishing developing the kingside and castling. Black seeks counterplay by pressuring b2, which White left undefended when they moved their bishop early on. (White does not want to take the offered c5 pawn of course: they'd rather play c3 and let Black trade into them, so that they can keep two pawns in the centre).

Having committed to d5 already, the King's Indian-style approach with 3...g6 is less common but still playable. Black continues 4...Bg7, and 5...O-O. White usually includes h3, so there is a retreat square for their bishop on h2, and Be2.

notes.text: You play Queen's Indian style: bishop to b7, then e6, Be7 and d6.
notes.original: 2...b6, to play Queen's Indian-style with ...Bb7, ...e6, ...Be7 and ...d6.

notes.text: You want Qb6 soon, to attack White's weak b2 pawn.
notes.original: 2...c5: after 3.e3 Qb6 Black wishes to target White's weak b2 pawn as soon as possible.

notes.text: White develops the knight to c3 so it can follow with e4 and grab the centre.
notes.original: White typically will play Nc3 instead of Nf3. This is so that they can try and get an early e4.

notes.text: Most London players choose this against you, but it's a mistake that leaves White's game not so good.
notes.original: This is the most common move by London System players against the Indian king defense. However, this is a mistake, as we call the game quickly, and White's game is not that good.

notes.text: Your d5 pawn stops e4 and steers play toward a Grünfeld-style position.
notes.original: Because of this, black should play d5 which now transposes into more of a Grünfeld position. This move stops e4 of course.

notes.text: Bg7 is a fine option if you don't mind White playing e4; engines dislike hypermodern setups, so ignore that.
notes.original: There is an option however to play Bg7 if black really doesn't want to play e4. The engines don't like it but the engines never like the KID or any hypermodern opening so this is irrelevant.

notes.text: Your rook and knight both pressure the weak e4 pawn.
notes.original: After the exchanges, we make Re8 to pressure the weak e4 pawn.

notes.text: White supports e4 with f3; bring your pieces to the attack and storm the kingside with pawns.
notes.original:
Now White supports e4 with f3. This is the position of the classic / normal variant of the Indian king defense.
In this position, you should have an idea of the game similar to the one I indicate with the arrows. That is, move the pieces to the attack, and create a storm of pawns on the kingside.

notes.text: Your a-pawn holds back White's b4 push, so your knight can settle on c5.
Your pawn attacks the bishop that pins your knight and makes it choose a square.
Unpin your queen, develop the bishop to d7, bring the b8 knight to c5, and move the f6 knight away…
notes.original: Now with the arrows, I show you how you should play in this position. That is, removing the queen from the bishop's pin, developing the bishop by d7, maneuvering the knight on b8 to c5, and removing the knight on f6 to make room for the pawn storm on the kingside.

notes.text: Your pawn challenges d4 and makes White decide whether to close or open the centre.
White pushes d5 and closes the centre.
notes.original: In this chapter we will see when White closes the center with d5.

notes.text: Now see how to play when White opens the centre with dxe5.
notes.original: Now let's see what happens and how we should play when White decides to open the center by dxe5.

notes.text: Your a-pawn guards b4, so a knight on c5 cannot be chased by White's b-pawn.
Your knight heads for c5, where it will hit the e4 pawn.
Your knight steps back so the f-pawn can advance to f5.
Your f-pawn strikes at e4 and starts your play on the kingside.
Your knight lands on c5, backed by the other knight, and adds pressure on e4.
You have more space on the kingside and a good position; bring your pieces there and use it.
notes.original: We now have space advantage on the kingside. The position is favorable for Black. Now you should play with a game plan similar to the one I show you with the arrows. That is, move the black pieces to the kingside, and take advantage of the space advantage to win the game.

notes.text: You win the pawn back, and your e5 pawn guards d4 and f4.
Your rook takes back the queen and now owns the open d-file.
Your knight leaves f6, so your bishop now attacks White's undefended knight on e5.
You take the knight back, and your bishop now threatens the unguarded b2 pawn.
You are much better and White can no longer castle long; develop your queenside pieces.
notes.original: Our tower controls column e. Now White cannot castle long. Black has a LOT of advantage. Now we must develop our queenside pieces as I show with the arrows.

notes.text: After you castle, White has a plan to follow, shown by the arrows.
notes.original: After castling, White plans to make the moves I show him with the arrows.

notes.text: In this Sämisch setup, White usually brings the queen out and castles long.
notes.original: In the Sämisch variant as shown with the arrows, White usually castle long.

notes.text: You will see Be3 far more often, but Bg5 is the second most common Sämisch move.
notes.original: Although you will see A LOT more Be3, this is the second most common move within the Sämisch variant.

notes.text: Remember: against short castling you play e5, against long castling you play c5, as here.
notes.original: Remember; When White castles short, we must do e5, and when he castles long, c5 as we did now.

notes.text: After your c5, White can close with d5, open with dxc5, or play Ne2, the most common and best.
notes.original: White after c5 has 3 options: close the center with d5, open it with dxc5, or Ne2, which is the most common and best move in this position.

notes.text: White closes the center with d5; let's see the most common plays and your answers.
notes.original:
With d5 White closes the center.
Let's see which are the most common plays and what we should do:

notes.text: White decides to open the center.
Your knight develops and joins the c5 pawn in pressing on d4.
White's pawn attacks your knight; e5 is its best square.
notes.original: What's the best square for this knight?

notes.text: Your queen pins the c3 knight to White's queen and backs up your c5 pawn.
Your knight escapes the pawn and threatens c4, which White's blocked bishop cannot guard.
Your e-pawn challenges White's d5 pawn, aiming to open the e-file for your rook.
Your rook lines up on the e-file before you trade pawns on d5.
Trading on d5 opens the e-file, so your rook now bears down on e4.
Your rook now has the open e-file, and you stand clearly better.
notes.original: Now our tower has an open column which is column e. We have a remarkable advantage in position.

notes.text: Taking back with the d-pawn opens the d-file, where your rook lands after queens trade.
Your rook takes back the queen and lands straight on the open d-file.
You have a big lead in development.
notes.original: We have a huge lead in development

notes.text: Your pawn attacks White's bishop on c5 and forces it to move away.
Your rook controls the open d-file, White cannot castle, and the position is very favorable for you.
notes.original:
Our rook controls the d-file and White cannot castle. The position is very, VERY favorable for the king india player.
Now your game idea should be similar to the one I indicate with the arrows.

notes.text: Your pawn attacks the bishop on g5 and makes it choose a square right away.
White again has dxc5, d5 or Ne2; answer as in the other Sämisch lines, now with your pawn on h6.
notes.original: Now White has 3 options: dxc5, d5, or Ne2. As you can see, it is the same position of the other 3 Sämisch variants that I have shown you previously, only now we have a pawn on h6. Depending on which option of the 3 white chooses, you will play as I have shown you in the other 3 Sämisch variants.

notes.text: Your bishop takes the long diagonal toward d4 and clears the way for castling.
Your pawn keeps White's knight out of e5 and prepares your own push there.
Your king gets safe behind the bishop before you decide how to hit the centre.
Your knight backs a pawn push to e5 or c5 against White's centre.
Your pawn makes room for the bishop to come out on b7.
White builds a pawn pyramid, but it doesn't help him and it suits you.
notes.original: White builds a pyramid of pawns, but this does not help him, and it benefits us.

notes.text: Your bishop takes the long diagonal and watches e4, the square White wants for its pawn.
Your rook stands behind the e-pawn, ready to back its push to e5.
Your pawn strikes at d4 and shuts the diagonal of White's bishop on h2.
Thanks to your d5 pawn, White cannot play e4 now.
notes.original: White is now unable to make e4 thanks to our move!

notes.text: Your bishop takes the long diagonal toward d4 and clears the way to castle.
White tries to open files by pushing the h-pawn.
notes.original: White tries to open files with the h-pawn

notes.text: With h5 you stop the h-pawn, so White cannot open files there.
notes.original: With h5 we anticipated and now they cannot open columns.

notes.text: Your king tucks in safely, since your h5 pawn keeps White's h-pawn stuck.
You take the pawn back, and the open d-file sets your queen against White's.
Your rook takes back the queen and lands on the open d-file.
Taking on e4 uncovers your bishop, which now attacks White's loose knight on e5.
Your bishop takes the knight back, so the pieces and pawns are level again.
Your setup is solid; play a6 and b5 to keep chipping away at White's center.
notes.original: Yes! We have a solid foundation. Our plans are a6 and b5, always trying to chip away at white's center.

notes.text: White's f4 starts the Four Pawns Attack; find your reply to the big pawn centre.
notes.original: What do we play?

notes.text: Break down White's centre with your c-pawn.
notes.original: Destroy white's center with c5!

notes.text: Your c-pawn strikes the d4 pawn and starts chipping at White's big centre.
Chip away at the centre with e6, then develop your knight via a5 and a6. Ugly, but it works.
notes.original: This seems scary, but if you know what you are doing, it's not. Chip away at white's center with e6, and to develop your b8-knight play a5-Na6. Ugly, but it does the job :) Once again, you have this safe kingside.

notes.text: Your bishop settles on the long diagonal and frees g8 for castling.
White is copying your setup; castle your king.
notes.original: Here is white copying you. Castle your king.

notes.text: Your king gets safe behind the bishop, and your rook comes to f8.
This is the one setup move you hadn't yet played; White now mirrors your setup.
notes.original: The only move of the setup you haven't played so far.

notes.text: Your d-pawn guards e5 and c5 and opens the diagonal for your light bishop.
Develop your knight to c6, the most common move.
notes.original: Continue with Nc6, it is the most common move.

notes.text: Your knight develops with pressure on the d4 pawn and backs a later e5 push.
Now play a6.
This prepares your rook to b8 and the b-pawn push against White's c4 pawn.
White's pawn attacks your knight; its best square is a5.
notes.original: You got attacked, the best square for the knight is on a5,

notes.text: On the rim your knight attacks the c4 pawn, which nothing defends yet.
The knight defends the c4 pawn; now gain space with c5.
notes.original: Nd2 defending the pawn. b3 doesn't work because of Ne4 and you win material. The move is c5 gaining space for your pieces.

notes.text: Good move. Aim for b5 on the queenside, and consider e6 and Bh6 to add pressure.
notes.original: Yes! Now you will play Rb1 and b5 with good play on the queenside. You should also consider e6 and Bh6 exerting pressure on the queenside. This will be a good game for you. Plans are highlighted.Also, please don't analyse this opening with the computer, it hates on the KID. Computers don't analyse the opening well, instead, pull up the book and compare your moves with master moves.

notes.text: Your king gets safe first, so you can strike at White's centre with the c-pawn.
Play c5 and destroy White's centre.
notes.original: The move here is c5. Destroy white's center!

notes.text: Your c-pawn attacks the d4 pawn and makes White decide what to do with its centre.
Chip away at White's centre with e6, then develop your knight via a5 and a6. This opening is sharp.
notes.original: Now, chip away at white's center with e6! Develop your b8-knight by playing a5-Na6. This opening is sharp!

notes.text: Your bishop pins the knight that guards White's d4 pawn.
White's h3 pawn attacks your bishop, which pins the knight on f3; White wants it gone.
notes.original: white wants to get rid of this bishop, because it is pinning the knight.

notes.text: You trade off the knight that guarded d4, so that pawn becomes your target.
Your knight attacks the d4 pawn, which has no defender left.
Your bishop and knight both hit the d4 pawn, so White must save it.
notes.original: double attack, white has to do something to save his pawn.

notes.text: Ne2 guards d4, but it lets your knight jump to e5 with a very nice move.
notes.original: white wanted to protect his pawn but now black can do a very nice move...

notes.text: Your knight hits the queen and bishop; it looks like a sacrifice, but you win the piece back.
notes.original: amazing! black temporary sacrifices his knight, but he will win it back later

You are winning: White lost castling, his queen is badly placed, and you will be two pawns up.
notes.original: black has a -4.0 advantage, black is about to be two pawns up, white has lost his castling privileges and white's queen is not on a good square.

Your attacked knight jumps away, hitting White's queen and bishop as it goes.
Your knight takes the bishop with check, leaving White with doubled c-pawns to guard.
Your rook backs the e-pawn, ready to break open the centre with e6.
You tuck your king away first, then hit the big centre with your c-pawn.
White cannot take on e5: after the queens come off, you end up with the better position.

Castling looks good, but your knight can take on e4 and win a pawn.
notes.original: this looks like a good move but black can now get a very nice position and win a pawn!

notes.original: we ignore the pin because we are attacking white's queen.

notes.original: not only did black win a pawn, but black also has a very good position. Black has a -4.2 advantage.

notes.text: You are a pawn up with a great position.
notes.original: black is up a pawn ad has a great position! Black has a -3.6 advantage

Moving the rook to e8 is a big blunder: it leaves f7 weak and White traps your queen.
notes.original: this is a big blunder

notes.original: amazing!

notes.original: this also works

notes.original: LOL! the queen is trapped!

notes.original: black cannot protect his pawn and his knight

notes.original: black is supposed to finish his fianchetto

notes.original: black plans to fianchetto his light squared bishop

notes.original: black has a nice pawn structure, but he has forgot something

Your knight retreats without blocking the d-file, and can go to c7 next.
Trading queens with check buys time to deal with the bishop's attack on your a8 rook.
Your knight covers the a8 rook, so taking it costs White its strong bishop.
White is a full rook up here.
notes.original: white is a rook up!

notes.text: This position can transpose, since White hasn't committed to c4 and you haven't chosen d5 or d6.
notes.original: A transposition position as White has yet to commit to playing c4, and Black has not committed the d-pawn to either d5 or d6.

notes.text: Challenge White's strong bishop with c5 or Nh5, then develop your pieces.
notes.original:
The London System is a solid and flexible opening system for white that can be played against various setups by black. After the moves:

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Nf6 3.e3 or

The main ideas for both sides in the London System's main line are:

Development and Structure: Nf3, Be2, c3, and often Nbd2 followed by a potential e4 break or the more restrained h3 and O-O. The pawn on d4 and the pawn on e3 provide a solid central structure.

Queenside Expansion: With moves like a4-a5 or a queenside pawn storm with b4, aiming for a potential minority attack.

King Safety: Usually achieved with O-O. The rook on f1 might later swing over to the c-file or e-file.

Central Break: Depending on Black's setup, White can aim for e4 at some point.

Challenge the Bishop: ...c5 or ...Nh5 can be played to challenge White's strong Bf4.

Development: e6 followed by Be7, O-O, and Nbd7 or Nc6. Depending on the situation, the light-squared bishop can be developed to d7, f5, or g4.

Central Control: Black usually maintains a pawn on d5 and can consider playing ...e5 under the right conditions.

Queenside Counterplay: Black can look for counterplay with moves like ...a6 and ...b5, depending on White's play. For a general introduction to the London System, take a closer look at 1.d4 d5 2.Bf4
